hints: Focus on how transition metal ions form, remember the 4s electrons are always removed before any 3d electrons.
Start with copper, atomic number 29 is $[Ar] 3d^{10} 4s^1$, so removing two electrons leaves a $3d^9$ configuration.
Now work out $Mn^{3+}$ and $V^{3+}$ as $3d^4$ and $3d^2$, then check if any d-subshell with 1 to 9 electrons can be fully paired.
walkthrough:
**Write the neutral atom configurations**

First, recall the atomic numbers and ground state configurations. Transition metals fill 4s before 3d.

$$Cu (29): [Ar] 3d^{10} 4s^1$$
$$Mn (25): [Ar] 3d^5 4s^2$$
$$V (23): [Ar] 3d^3 4s^2$$

**Form the ions by removing 4s first**

When forming positive ions, we remove from 4s first, then from 3d. This is the key rule students often forget.

$$Cu^{2+}: [Ar] 3d^9$$
$$Mn^{3+}: [Ar] 3d^4$$
$$V^{3+}: [Ar] 3d^2$$

**Count unpaired electrons**

A d-subshell holds 5 orbitals, so electrons stay unpaired as far as possible. Any $d^1$ to $d^9$ must have at least one unpaired electron.

$Cu^{2+}$ is $d^9$ with 1 unpaired, $Mn^{3+}$ is $d^4$ with 4 unpaired, $V^{3+}$ is $d^2$ with 2 unpaired. So 1, 2 and 3 are all correct.

options.A: Correct, because all three ions have partially filled d-subshells. $Cu^{2+}$ is $3d^9$ (1 unpaired), $Mn^{3+}$ is $3d^4$ (4 unpaired) and $V^{3+}$ is $3d^2$ (2 unpaired).
options.B: Incorrect. This combination suggests only 1 and 2 are correct and excludes $V^{3+}$. $V^{3+}$ is $[Ar] 3d^2$, so its two 3d electrons occupy separate orbitals unpaired.
options.C: Incorrect. This combination suggests only 2 and 3 are correct and excludes $Cu^{2+}$. $Cu^{2+}$ is $[Ar] 3d^9$, which clearly leaves one unpaired electron in the 3d set.
options.D: Incorrect. This suggests only 1 is correct. It ignores that $Mn^{3+}$ ($3d^4$) and $V^{3+}$ ($3d^2$) also have multiple unpaired d-electrons.
